Visible injuries or wounds on others

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.

I have permanently changed for the worse

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' conflicts with the same node's strong intrusive, poorly controlled re-experiencing items ('triggered without warning' and 'full sensory reliving'). Severe reliving can coexist with disclosure, but 'very easily' pulls in the opposite direction and is the clearest within-node inconsistency.

issues.item: Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
issues.explanation: The cognitive formulation leaves Threat disconnected from the active network, yet 'Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time' implies a strong ongoing sense of current threat. That threat-focused appraisal is not supported by the formulation and is not matched by any Threat-node content.

issues.item: Memory: Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
issues.explanation: 'Entrapment: Having no options' as a trigger is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The negative appraisals and memory content center on global damage/self-reliance and sensory reliving, not on themes of being trapped or unable to escape, so this trigger appears insufficiently grounded in the reported formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Physical Stress' is weakly supported by the rest of the profile. The triggers and appraisals do not indicate body-strain or exertion as a salient trauma-linked theme, making this strategy look disconnected from the reported trigger-memory-appraisal pattern.

The trigger profile is centered on entrapment, touch, and a specific taste, which implies reactivity to concrete sensory or situational reminders of the witnessed trauma. 'Entrapment: Having no options' is harder to reconcile with the rest of the profile because the memory and appraisal items do not describe being trapped or immobilized; they emphasize sensory reliving, nonverbal memory, hypervigilance, and global damage/self-doubt rather than a trapped-state theme. For a witnessed-trauma case, this item stands out as poorly integrated with the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Physical Stress: Situations that put my body under stress
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Physical Stress' is not well supported by the rest of the five-component profile. The selected triggers and memory items point to sensory cue-driven reliving, and the appraisals concern vigilance, self-reliance, and life damage. Avoiding bodily stress suggests fear of physiological arousal or somatic activation, but there are no corresponding threat or appraisal items about bodily danger, losing control when activated, or physical collapse. It therefore looks like a maladaptive strategy targeting a symptom pattern not otherwise represented in the profile.

issues.item: Avoid Reminders: Being reminded of the event by others
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Reminders' appears mis-keyed: the strategy should be an avoidant behavior (e.g., avoiding being reminded), but the selected text describes a trigger/reminder rather than something the patient does. This makes the maladaptive-strategy item internally incoherent.

issues.item: Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time
issues.explanation: The profile includes a prominent current-threat appraisal ('I have to be on guard all the time') despite Threat being structurally inactive: there are no active edges to or from Threat, and the rest of the profile is dominated by memory-based reexperiencing, negative self-appraisals, and coping strategies rather than an active external-danger formulation. This item fits Threat more than Negative Appraisals and is inconsistent with the specified formulation.

vignette:
David sits in the chair with the stillness of a man trying not to disturb the air around him. At thirty, his carpenter’s hands, usually steady and capable, rest uncertainly on his knees. The story of the last eight months doesn’t come easily; for him, the event isn't a narrative he can recount but a physical state he falls back into. He explains that he can’t seem to put the frightening parts into words, that they exist as a knot of sensation just below his throat. It began on a Tuesday at a residential job site. He was on a short break, leaning against a stack of lumber and sipping a hot, sweet hazelnut coffee from a thermos, when he heard the shout, followed by a sickening thud. His friend and colleague, Marco, had fallen from the second-story scaffolding.

David was the first one there. The memory, when it comes for him now, is never a simple recollection. It arrives without warning, a complete sensory ambush. He’ll be at home and his wife, Sarah, will gently touch his arm, and suddenly it is no longer her hand but the horrifyingly slick, warm feeling of Marco’s blood on his own as he tried to apply pressure to the wound on his leg. The sight of the exposed bone, stark white against the crimson, is an image that can flash into his mind if he sees so much as a child with a scraped knee at the park. When these moments hit, it feels completely real. He’s back on the dusty ground, the smell of sawdust in the air, the cloying taste of hazelnut coffee still coating his tongue as he tries not to be sick. The world of his living room dissolves, replaced by the full, terrifying reality of that moment.

In the weeks that followed the accident, David began to change. He had come to believe that he was fundamentally broken, that the trauma had permanently altered him for the worse. This certainty settled deep inside him, colouring every interaction. He stopped drinking coffee entirely, the taste now a potent trigger. He began flinching from Sarah’s touch, pulling away from the very comfort he needed, because any physical contact could send him spiraling. Confused and hurt, she started keeping her distance, and a quiet chasm opened between them. At work, he became a liability. A coworker nicked his hand with a utility knife, and the sight of the small beads of blood sent David into a state of near-paralysis. He just stood there, staring, until his foreman shook him and sent him home. He started deliberately trying to make his mind go blank when he felt a memory approaching, staring fixedly at a point on the wall until the world fuzzed out at the edges, a strategy that left him feeling even more disconnected.

The conviction that he could no longer rely on himself became absolute. He, who had always been so dependable, now felt like a stranger in his own body. To manage the constant, thrumming anxiety, he began to eat. At night, long after Sarah was asleep, he would go to the kitchen and consume food without tasting it—a whole box of cereal, a bag of chips, anything to fill the gnawing emptiness and quiet the noise in his head. He avoided talking or even thinking about what happened, believing that if he just pushed it down hard enough, it might eventually stay buried. But this only seemed to give the memories more power when they inevitably broke through. He felt as though his life, the one he had carefully built with his hands and his heart, had been completely destroyed. The capable man, the loving husband, was gone, replaced by this fragile, frightened shell. It was Sarah who finally brought him here. Last week, after he recoiled from her attempt at a hug, she had looked at him with tears in her eyes and said, “I miss you, David. I don’t know where you’ve gone.” He is here now because he is terrified that she is right, and that he will never find his way back.
